metaDescription: Generative engine optimization means getting cited inside AI answers. Most of it is the SEO you should already be doing — here are the three new parts.
definition: Generative engine optimization is the practice of getting your content retrieved, quoted and cited inside AI-generated answers rather than ranked in a list of blue links.
answer: Generative engine optimization is the work of getting cited inside AI-generated answers from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and AI Overviews. Roughly four-fifths of it is ordinary SEO — crawlable pages, clear structure, genuine authority. The genuinely new parts are quotable phrasing, off-site presence on the sources models retrieve, and measuring citations instead of ranks.
takeaways: The term comes from a 2023 academic paper, not from an agency. Anyone selling it as a proprietary method is selling you a research abstract.
Most of GEO is SEO. If your site isn't crawlable and doesn't rank, there is nothing for a model to retrieve.
Three things are actually new: **quotable phrasing**, **off-site presence where models look**, and **citation as the unit of measurement**.
There is no rank tracker for this. You measure with a repeatable prompt panel and referral data, and you accept the noise.

body: GEO was coined in a 2023 research paper titled **GEO: Generative Engine Optimization**, from researchers at Princeton, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI and IIT Delhi. They tested how editing a page changed its visibility inside generative answers, and found that adding citations, direct quotations and statistics tended to improve how often and how prominently a source was used — while classic keyword stuffing did not.

That's the honest provenance. It is a research direction with early empirical support, not a mature discipline with settled best practice. Treat anyone claiming a proven GEO playbook with the scepticism you'd apply to a proven playbook for a search engine that launched last year.

sections.h2: The part that's just SEO wearing a new hat
body: Generative engines don't hallucinate your website into existence. They retrieve — from a search index, from their own crawl, from a live query to Bing or Google. Which means the entry requirements are the ones you already know.
If you skip this list and buy a GEO package instead, you are paying a premium for the second half of a job whose first half is missing.
bullets: **Crawlable and indexable.** If Googlebot and the AI crawlers can't fetch it, nothing downstream matters. Check your [robots.txt](/glossary/robots-txt) actually permits the assistants you want to be cited by.
**Ranking already.** Sources cited in AI answers overwhelmingly come from pages already visible for the query. Page-one presence remains the entry fee.
**Clear structure.** Headings that describe their content, short paragraphs, tables for comparisons. Retrieval works on chunks, and a wall of text chunks badly.

**Real authority.** [Topical authority](/glossary/topical-authority) and consistent entity signals matter more here, not less — a model choosing between five sources leans on the same reputation cues as a ranking system.
**Accurate, dated facts.** Models prefer specific, verifiable, recent claims over adjectives.

sections.h2: The three things that are genuinely new
body: Strip out everything that's ordinary SEO and this is what remains. It's a short list, which is exactly why we don't sell it as a separate product.

A model extracts a passage, not a page. So every important claim needs to survive being cut out of its context — self-contained, subject named rather than pronouned, number attached where a number exists.

Practically: define the term in the first sentence under the heading, put comparisons in tables rather than prose, and attribute statistics to a nameable source in the same sentence. That last habit is the one the original research pointed at most clearly.

subs.h3: 2. Be present where models retrieve, not just on your own site
body: Assistants pull heavily from places you don't own — community threads, review platforms, industry directories, YouTube transcripts, documentation sites. A brand with no third-party footprint is invisible to a retrieval step no matter how good its own pages are.
This is closer to digital PR than to technical SEO, and it makes [brand mentions](/glossary/brand-mentions) without links genuinely valuable for the first time.

AI crawlers are separate user agents from Googlebot, and blocking them is a real decision with real trade-offs — no citation without access. Most businesses selling something should let them in; publishers monetising pageviews have a legitimate argument the other way.

sections.h2: Citation is the unit, and it's hard to count
body: There is no average position in a generative answer. Either you were used as a source or you weren't, and the same prompt can produce different sources twice in a row. That non-determinism breaks every measurement habit built over twenty years of rank tracking.

What works instead is cruder and more honest. Build a fixed panel of 30 to 50 prompts a real buyer would type, run them on a schedule across the assistants you care about, and log whether you appear and in what role. It's sampling, it's noisy, and it's still the best available signal.

Alongside that, watch referral sessions from assistant domains in [GA4](/glossary/google-analytics-4) — small volumes today for most Indian sites, but the trend line is worth owning early. And accept the ceiling: a citation with no click still shifted a buyer's shortlist, and nothing in your analytics will ever show it.

callout.title: What we won't sell you
callout.body: We don't invoice GEO as a separate retainer line, because roughly four-fifths of the work is the SEO you're already paying for. It runs inside the SEO engagement. If you want the specifics of what that includes, [AEO and GEO services](/services/aeo-geo-services) sets it out — but the honest pitch is that it's a change of emphasis, not a new product.

faqs.q: What's the difference between GEO and SEO?
faqs.a: SEO aims at a position in a list of links; GEO aims at being the source an AI answer quotes. The underlying work overlaps heavily — crawlability, structure, authority — because generative engines retrieve from search indexes. GEO adds quotable phrasing, off-site presence and citation-based measurement.

faqs.q: Is GEO worth paying extra for?
faqs.a: As a separate retainer, usually not. Most of what a GEO package contains is standard SEO with different vocabulary. What's worth insisting on is that your existing SEO work includes liftable formatting, third-party presence and a prompt-panel measurement habit — three additions, not a second invoice.

faqs.q: How do I get cited by ChatGPT or Perplexity?
faqs.a: Rank for the query first, since retrieval mostly draws from pages already visible. Then make the answer extractable: a direct definition under a question-shaped heading, specific numbers with named sources, comparisons in tables. Then build presence on the third-party sites and communities models pull from.

faqs.q: Does GEO have anything to do with local SEO?
faqs.a: No, despite the acronym clash. GEO here means generative engine optimization. Geographic or local SEO is an entirely separate discipline about map packs, Google Business Profiles and city-level ranking. The overlapping abbreviation is unfortunate and increasingly common in briefs.

faqs.q: Can I track GEO results the way I track rankings?
faqs.a: Not reliably. Generative answers are non-deterministic, so the same prompt can cite different sources minutes apart. The practical substitute is a fixed panel of buyer-realistic prompts, run on a schedule, logging appearance rate — plus referral traffic from assistant domains as a secondary signal.
